sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Cumberland County
sections.html:
Cumberland County Tax Administration assesses real estate and sends the bills. The office is on the fifth floor of the county courthouse in downtown Fayetteville, Room 530, 117 Dick Street. The phone number is 910-678-7507, and it is the same number you call to set up a payment plan.

The department's website covers the topics a seller usually needs: revaluation, real estate appeals, exemptions and exclusions, tax relief programs, payment plans, delinquent taxes, a surplus property list and tax foreclosure sales.

About 338,473 people live in the county, in 146,623 housing units. Owners occupy 55.0% of homes, so close to half the housing is rental, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $199,200. Rates differ from one town to the next, so the address matters when you estimate what a buyer will pay each year.

On 2026 bills (fiscal year 2027) the county's general rate is 49.9 cents per $100 of valuation, with a 5.0-cent special recreation rate beside it. Towns add their own rates, so the total depends on where the parcel sits.

sections.h2: Flat fees on the tax bill
sections.html:
Several service charges ride on the same bill, outside the rate. The county prints these amounts:

  • Solid waste fee of $285 a year for Fayetteville residences with seven or fewer units.
  • Solid waste fee of $130 a year for unincorporated areas and every municipality except Spring Lake.
  • Refuse tax of $342.72 a year in Hope Mills and $396.00 in Spring Lake, the latter including a $12 residential litter control fee.
  • Fayetteville residential storm water by impervious surface: $84.00 below 2,500 square feet, $168.00 for 2,501 to 4,800, $252.00 beyond that.
  • Residential storm water of $60 a year in Spring Lake and in Hope Mills.
  • Vehicle fees: $25 vehicle fee plus a $5 transit tax in Fayetteville, $10 in Hope Mills, and $5 each in Stedman and Spring Lake.

A buyer comparing your house to another will look at the whole bill, so read it line by line. Moving across a town line can change the charges more than the home's value does.

Bills are due September 1. Pay by January 5 and there is no interest, penalty or collection action.

After that, state law (G.S. 105-360) adds 2% starting January 6, then three-fourths of one percent for each month or fraction from February 1. MyCCNCPay takes credit, debit or electronic draft payments. A payment plan goes through the phone number above.

Property listing closes January 31 each year under G.S. 105-307. Anything that changed on your parcel, such as new construction, gets reported by then.

Unpaid bills can end in a tax foreclosure sale. An outside attorney runs those sales for the tax office, and the county's foreclosure page names that attorney and shows parcels in an upset bid period. Until the court confirms the sale, an owner can still redeem by paying the taxes, penalties, interest and costs (G.S. 105-374).

Real property was reappraised countywide for 2025, eight years after the January 1, 2017 revaluation. The county follows an eight-year cycle under G.S. 105-286, so expect the next one on that schedule.

A revaluation year runs in a set order. Notices go to owners in February, and the notice carries an informal appeal form on its back. Informal appeals are due in March, the Board of Equalization and Review convenes in April, and formal appeals close in May when the board adjourns. New rates using the updated values take effect July 1, and bills follow that August.

Owners who agree with the notice need not respond. Assessed values are posted online, and a Revaluation Call Center at 910-678-7800 books appointments with appraisers. The county also points owners to three state relief programs: present use deferment, the elderly or disabled exclusion and the disabled veteran exclusion.

Start with an informal review, then send a formal request to the Board of Equalization and Review before it adjourns. You can deliver it to Room 543 of the courthouse, mail it to PO Box 449 in Fayetteville (ZIP 28302), or use the secure drop box on the courthouse's rear lot.

Requests must be in writing. An appraiser contacts every taxpayer who appeals, and a letter sets the hearing date and time if the case goes to the board. Useful evidence includes appraisals, comparable properties, income and expense statements, repair cost estimates and photos of unusual conditions.

The regular board's first meeting falls between the first Monday in April and the first Monday in May. Outside a revaluation year it wraps up by the third Monday after starting, unless it needs longer, and it cannot sit past July 1. In 2026 the board convened April 22 and took real property appeals until it adjourned May 20.

A special board meets at 3:30 p.m. on the second Wednesday of each month except July and approves corrections, clerical errors included. If you disagree with a board decision, you have 30 days from the mailing of the notice to appeal to the state Property Tax Commission (G.S. 105-290).

sections.h2: Exclusions that can lower the bill
sections.html:
The disabled veteran exclusion removes the first $45,000 of appraised value. There is no age or income test. A Veterans Service Officer completes Form NCDVA-9 first, and the form then goes to the assessor.

Elderly or disabled relief and the circuit breaker go through Form AV-9 at the assessor, accepted up to June 1. If you qualify, mention it when you list the house, because a lower annual bill is a selling point for the next owner.

Taxes are a lien on the property, so an unpaid bill does not go away at closing. The closing attorney normally pays what is owed out of your proceeds and gets a payoff figure from Tax Administration first. Call 910-678-7507 for the amount, since interest grows each month after January 5.

If the house is already in the foreclosure process, you still have the right to redeem until the court confirms the sale. A buyer paying cash can close quickly enough to clear the taxes before that point, and a cash sale skips the lender appraisal and loan approval steps that slow a financed one.

Bring the latest tax bill, any exemption approvals and your payment history to the first meeting with your attorney. Mid-year sales are common, so ask Tax Administration how the current bill is split between you and the buyer.

faqs.q: When are Cumberland County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Every September 1. January 5 is the last day to pay before interest, and the 2% charge starts January 6.

faqs.q: What is the combined rate inside Fayetteville city limits?
faqs.a: The City of Fayetteville rate is 0.4495 and the county rate is 0.499, for a combined 0.9485 per $100 on 2026 bills.

faqs.q: Where does a formal appeal go?
faqs.a: Take it to Room 543 of the courthouse, mail it to PO Box 449, or use the secure drop box. It must be in writing and in hand before the board adjourns.

faqs.q: When was the last Cumberland County revaluation?
faqs.a: The 2025 revaluation is the latest. The one before it took effect January 1, 2017, and the county revalues every eight years.

faqs.q: Who runs Cumberland County tax foreclosure sales?
faqs.a: An outside attorney conducts them for the Tax Office. Call the attorney's office listed on the county's foreclosure page for sale dates and upset bid status.
